feature1.prompt: When running Django with an ASGI server such as uvicorn, the first middleware in the MIDDLEWARE list receives a coroutine instead of an HttpResponse. In a typical reproduction, a dummy middleware that prints the types of its arguments shows that when placed first the response is a coroutine, while moving the middleware down results in an HttpResponse. This issue has been noted to affect packages like django-cors-headers that are frequently positioned first. The goal is to ensure that middleware initialization works uniformly so that every middleware receives the expected HttpResponse regardless of its ordering.
feature1.hint_texts: This feature involves refactoring the middleware initialization logic. The changes should replace the legacy deprecation handling (using self._get_response_none_deprecation and manual assignment of get_response) with a clean call to super().__init__(get_response) for the affected middleware classes. Focus on updating the __init__ methods in the session, cache, and security middleware so that the new initialization pattern is applied consistently. This refactoring will remove deprecated code and improve maintainability.
feature1.entrypoint: Files to modify include: django/contrib/sessions/middleware.py (SessionMiddleware.__init__), django/middleware/cache.py (UpdateCacheMiddleware.__init__, FetchFromCacheMiddleware.__init__, and CacheMiddleware.__init__), and django/middleware/security.py (SecurityMiddleware.__init__). Look for code blocks that call self._get_response_none_deprecation(get_response) and assign self.get_response manually, and replace them with calls to super().__init__(get_response).

feature2.prompt: When using an ASGI server and configuring middleware in Django, shifting the position of a middleware in the MIDDLEWARE list changes the type of response received by its process_response method. Specifically, a dummy middleware placed first logs a coroutine instead of an HttpResponse, while moving it later corrects the type to HttpResponse. This discrepancy, which has been linked to issues in packages like django-cors-headers, highlights a need to handle coroutine responses correctly. The objective is to ensure that middleware consistently manages asynchronous responses, regardless of their placement in the middleware chain.
feature2.hint_texts: This feature focuses on enhancing the test suite to confirm proper behavior when middleware processes asynchronous responses. Developers should add new tests that simulate scenarios with async get_response functions and verify that the middleware either treats the response as a coroutine or as a synchronous HttpResponse appropriately. Concentrate on creating tests that trigger deprecation warnings when None is passed to the get_response argument and that identify coroutine behavior in the middleware’s initialization.
feature2.entrypoint: The modifications should be made in the test file tests/deprecation/test_middleware_mixin.py. Add new test methods, such as test_deprecation (to confirm that a deprecation warning is raised under improper usage) and test_coroutine (to check that the middleware instance responds as a coroutine when supplied with an async get_response). Verify that these tests are integrated properly with the overall test suite.

collaboration_points.shared_resources: Both features affect and rely on the Django middleware framework, especially the __init__ methods implemented in middleware files and the configuration in the MIDDLEWARE setting. They share the same middleware classes and settings used in both production and test environments.
collaboration_points.integration_strategy: Feature1 will refactor and standardize the middleware initialization while Feature2 will add tests to validate that the response types are handled correctly. The final integration requires that the refactored middleware code supports both synchronous and asynchronous (coroutine) behaviors as expected by the test suite.
collaboration_points.communication_needs: Developers working on Feature1 and Feature2 must coordinate to ensure that the refactoring does not break existing functionality and that the new tests in Feature2 adequately cover the changes. Regular discussions during code reviews and integration meetings will be essential to verify that both the middleware behavior and its test coverage align with the intended improvements.
